verdict: Lend selectively to Panaji's cash-rich, safety-compliant hotels and restaurants; the data pack gives no score, so treat this as a Caution call and lean on structure and monthly cash discipline rather than headline growth.
title: Panaji Tourism, Hotels & Restaurants: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
A Panaji hotel or restaurant buys rooms, kitchen, staff and licences, then sells nights and covers. **Cash arrives daily at the counter, but the cost base is fixed and monthly, so the whole credit rests on peak-season collections covering the lean months.** Value sits in location, licence and repeat guests, not in the building. Capex is heavy and lumpy (refurbishment, kitchen, safety systems); working capital is short and mostly negative if deposits are taken. **So when a proposal lands, check the seasonality of collections against the fixed-cost run-rate; if the lean-month cover is thin, ask for the last two years' monthly bank statements.**

## What has changed now
Local reporting is entirely about safety enforcement ahead of the peak season: police and the tourism department are stepping up measures [1], and hotels and clubs have been told to raise safety standards [2]. **That is a compliance cost and an operating condition, not a demand signal; budget for it in the proposal.** Peer results are strong but from large listed chains, not Panaji SMEs: ITC Hotels Q2 FY27 consolidated revenue Rs 1,054 crore, up 26 percent, EBITDA Rs 337 crore up 37 percent [3]; Ventive Q3 FY26 revenue up 27 percent with 48 percent EBITDA margin [4]; Leela Q2 with 30 percent RevPAR growth, entirely ARR-led [5]. **These tell us pricing power exists at the top end; they say nothing about Panaji's mid-market, and the sources are silent on this city, so lean on first principles.**

## Where to grow
Pursue owner-operated hotels and restaurants with a clean safety record, documented deposits, and a mixed domestic and MICE book. **The peer evidence points to ARR-led growth and MICE demand [5], so favour borrowers who can show room-rate realisation and event bookings, not just occupancy.** Avoid single-property borrowers with no cushion, venues with unresolved safety notices [2], and anyone whose cash is collected off-book. **If a borrower cannot show monthly cash deposits matching declared sales, ask for the collection account to be routed through us before sanction.**

## How to grow safely
Structure against the season: limit tenor to the peak cycle, take a charge on receivables and the licence, and set a debt-service cover tested on lean-month collections. **Take monthly stock and sales statements, bank statements and a safety-compliance certificate every month; if any month's deposit falls below the agreed floor, ask for the reason in writing and freeze further drawdown.** Capex loans only against quotations and completed work. **Collect from customer the actual occupancy, ARR and F&B split; the pack carries no Panaji figures.**

## Early-warning signs
Watch for falling counter deposits in the run-up to peak season, staff attrition, and any fresh safety notice [1][2]. **If deposits drop two months running or a notice lands, move to a stock-and-receivables audit and reprice.** Rating reports note liquidity and promoter support as key tests [8]; apply the same lens to the promoter's other businesses.
